requirements.statement: The first intake slice accepts local HTML, Markdown, and plain-text files.
Intake emits a deterministic, versioned `SourceBundle` containing source identity, format, raw SHA-256 digest, and ordered text blocks.
Every block has a stable ID, source line, block kind, section path, and normalized text.
Intake performs no network request and makes no claim that extracted text is a correct requirement or specification.
AI or human synthesis remains outside the deterministic core and communicates through versioned files.
The repository uses its own graph and proof mechanism on its source, specification, design, tests, implementation, and evidence.
The first external acceptance source may not introduce source-specific extraction rules into the product.
A requirement proposal is a provider-neutral artifact that binds every candidate and question to current `SourceBundle` blocks.
The core validates proposal provenance and structure without deciding whether a proposed statement is semantically correct.
Human review is recorded separately from the proposal, binds to the exact reviewable candidate content, and can accept or reject requirements and resolve questions.
The core reports whether review is blocked or ready for specification materialization and identifies every outstanding decision.
External AI and document-generation adapters communicate through versioned files; the core does not load a provider SDK or execute adapter commands.
The repository uses the proposal, review, and status protocols to develop this workflow slice itself.
The product discovers installed agent CLIs through safe capability and login-status probes and never reads or copies their OAuth tokens.
An explicit project adapter selection wins; automatic selection is allowed only when exactly one authenticated compatible adapter is available.
Starting from one supported source creates a self-contained workspace, deterministic `SourceBundle`, AI requirement proposal, and review gate.
After review, the selected adapter produces a structured development plan from which the core deterministically materializes `SPEC.md`, `TEST_SPEC.md`, `DESIGN.md`, and an implementation plan.
An explicit implementation action delegates workspace changes to the authenticated agent and records the adapter, reviewed plan, changed artifacts, and reported checks.
An explicit verification action runs only reviewed argv-style commands without a shell, captures their outputs and exit codes, and records fresh graph evidence.
The first complete product accepts local HTML, Markdown, text, and text-bearing PDF sources; OCR remains an external reader capability.
A project cannot report terminal completion until source, proposal, review, materialization, implementation, verification, and evidence nodes all exist and are current.
The repository develops every new slice through its own latest usable workflow and promotes dogfood failures into product contracts and regression tests.
Review decisions bind to individual candidate digests so unchanged decisions survive proposal growth while new or changed candidates become explicit blockers.
Development planning binds to reviewed project context such as an existing language, framework, source boundary, and constraints, and the core rejects silent architecture replacement.
An optional executable-contract adapter may pin an exact external compiler revision without making that compiler or its runtime a dependency of the Go core or released binary.

Mermaid contracts use stable contract identities and explicit implementation, test, consumer, and documentation links; missing, duplicate, unknown, or repository-escaping links fail verification instead of being inferred.
A contract change can produce bounded context and propagated impact artifacts for a context-free agent, including affected contracts, linked implementation files, and linked tests.
Targeted impact tests are advisory; terminal completion still requires regenerated artifacts, compiler drift verification, the reviewed full verification suite, and fresh graph evidence.

Publication is a separate explicit boundary that exposes only allowlisted repository artifacts, stores portable adapter provenance, excludes transient context, and rejects local user paths, credential-shaped material, symlinks, binary content, and oversized files before upload.
GroundSpec is publicly reusable under the MIT license through a stable Go install path, versioned self-contained binaries, checksums, and a CI-verified source build.
A user can initialize GroundSpec in an existing non-empty project without overwriting existing files, while reserved workflow-path conflicts fail closed.
The workflow helps a human and an AI move from source evidence to specifications, design, tests, implementation, and fresh verification evidence without hiding assumptions or unresolved decisions.
The deterministic core must not silently convert an inferred requirement into fact.
The v0 product does not ingest images or audio and does not provide built-in OCR ingestion.
The v0 product does not guarantee that a hiring assignment or product review will pass.
A contract-to-file link alone must not be treated as proof that an AI change is semantically correct.
The v0 product does not automatically upload, commit, or push artifacts.
